Falkland sprat (Sprattus fuegensis) reaches a maximum total length of 18 cm [Li = 18 cm], a size that is comparatively modest among clupeiform fishes but typical for small pelagics inhabiting cool South Atlantic waters. Body mass at the ultimate length has been estimated at 21.4 grams [Wwi = 21.4 grams], based on length-weight relationships established for local populations. This species exhibits a relatively short lifespan; field records and otolith-based ageing studies indicate that individuals live for approximately 12 years [am = approximately 12 years] when maintained at a mean annual water temperature of 7.8 °C [T = 7.8 °C], a thermal regime characteristic of the Falkland shelf region. The observed longevity is somewhat greater than that reported for the closely related European sprat (Sprattus sprattus), which rarely exceeds 6 years in northern waters, suggesting that cooler temperatures may decelerate the senescence process in this lineage. Sprat schools are heavily exploited by local fisheries, making accurate life-history parameters essential for stock assessment models. The 18 cm [Li = 18 cm] asymptotic length represents an upper boundary rarely encountered in contemporary catches, as fishing pressure selectively removes larger, older individuals from the population.

Puberty in Falkland sprat occurs at a total length of 12 cm [Lp = 12 cm], corresponding to a body mass of approximately 6.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 6.3 grams] as derived from the regional length-mass regression. These values are consistent with those documented for European sprat, for which the same pubertal length has been reported, suggesting a conserved size threshold for reproductive maturation within the genus. The mass of 6.3 grams [Wwp = 6.3 grams] at maturity represents roughly 29 percent of the ultimate body mass, a proportion that aligns with expectations for a small, fast-growing clupeid. Upon first reaching this size, gonadal recrudescence is initiated, and spawning can commence within the same breeding season. The transition to reproductive competence is likely triggered by a combination of somatic growth attainment and photoperiodic cues, although the precise endocrine mechanisms remain understudied for this species. Understanding the size at puberty is critical for fisheries management, as it directly informs minimum landing sizes and spawning stock biomass calculations.

Neonatal Falkland sprat emerge from pelagic eggs at a weight of just 0.00051 grams [Wwb = 0.00051 grams], a mass derived from the typical egg diameter of 0.99 mm and reflecting the small oocyte size characteristic of broadcast-spawning clupeids. The freshly hatched yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during its first days post-eclosion, with the duration of this lecithotrophic phase depending strongly on ambient temperature. Under the cool conditions of the Falkland Current, yolk absorption proceeds relatively slowly, allowing the prolarva to attain a more advanced developmental stage before it must locate prey. The minuscule birth mass of 0.00051 grams [Wwb = 0.00051 grams] imposes a very narrow window for successful first feeding; once the yolk is exhausted, the larva must encounter suitable zooplankton within hours or risk starvation mortality. This high early-life vulnerability is a major bottleneck in the population dynamics of small pelagic fishes and helps explain the enormous fecundity required to sustain stable adult numbers.

Reproductive output in Falkland sprat is substantial, with females carrying a relative fecundity of 288 eggs per gram of body weight. For an average mature female of 21.4 grams [Wwi = 21.4 grams], this translates to a batch fecundity of roughly 6,160 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 6,160 eggs per spawning event]. Given that spawning likely occurs at intervals of several days over an extended breeding season, with females potentially producing as many as 10 batches per year [F_R_i = 10 batches per year], the overall reproductive output under the prevailing thermal regime of 7.8 °C [T = 7.8 °C] is considerable. The congeneric Sprattus sprattus, upon which some demographic parameters are based, produces multiple batches per season, and a similar iteroparous strategy is presumed for the Falkland species. Pelagic eggs are released directly into the water column, where fertilisation occurs externally. The high fecundity of approximately 6,160 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 6,160 eggs per clutch] compensates for the substantial egg and larval mortality inherent in a pelagic life history, ensuring that sufficient offspring survive to replace the parental generation each year.

Males of Falkland sprat typically weigh around 6.3 grams [Wwp = around 6.3 grams] upon reaching puberty, mirroring the female size at maturation, while the maximum adult body mass for both sexes converges at 21.4 grams [Wwi = 21.4 grams]. The total lifespan of 12 years [am = 12 years] at a mean temperature of 7.8 °C [T = 7.8 °C] places this species among the longer-lived sprats, a longevity that may be linked to the relatively slow metabolic rates characteristic of cold-water clupeids. Growth increments after maturity become progressively smaller, with asymptotic length attained only after several years. The species faces predation pressure from seabirds, marine mammals, and larger piscivorous fish throughout its life, but the high reproductive rate ensures population resilience. Fisheries catch data from the Falkland Islands show that sprats constitute a key forage species in the regional food web, linking primary productivity to higher trophic levels. Continued monitoring of body size distributions and reproductive parameters is essential for sustainable management of this valuable marine resource.
